title: Problem Statement and Historical Context
content:
Erdős Problem #434 asks: Which k-element subset of {1,...,n} maximizes the count of non-representable integers (sums with repetition)? Kiss (2002) proved the answer is {n-k+1,...,n} (the 'top k' set).

This connects to the classical Frobenius/coin problem: given coin denominations with gcd 1, what amounts can't be made? Problem #434 goes further — it optimizes the *choice* of denominations to maximize unreachable amounts.

mathContext.historicalNote: The Frobenius problem dates to Frobenius (1882) and Sylvester (1884). Erdős and Graham posed the extremal variant in their 1980 monograph. Kiss solved it in 2002 in Ann. Univ. Sci. Budapest.

crossReferences.relationship: Problem #433 asks for the maximum Frobenius NUMBER for k-element subsets; #434 asks for maximum COUNT of non-representables. Related extremal problems from the same Erdős-Graham monograph.

title: Representability via Multisets
content:
**IsRepresentableAs n A** holds when n = a₁ + a₂ + ... + aₘ for some aᵢ ∈ A (repetition allowed). Formalized using `Multiset ℕ`: there exists S with all elements in A and S.sum = n.

Examples with A = {3, 5}: 6 = 3+3 (representable), 8 = 3+5 (representable), 7 (NOT representable).

This is the numerical semigroup generated by A: the set of all nonneg integer linear combinations.

mathContext.technique: Existential over Multiset ℕ with membership constraint (∀ a ∈ S, a ∈ A) and sum constraint (S.sum = n)
consequences: mem_representable: elements of A are representable (singleton multiset)
add_representable: representability is closed under addition (multiset concatenation)
mathContext.keyProperty: The representable set forms a numerical semigroup (closed under addition, containing 0)

title: Zero is Always Representable
content:
**zero_representable**: 0 is representable by any set A, using the empty multiset ∅ with sum 0. Proved by `use ∅; simp`.

This is the identity element of the numerical semigroup: the empty sum convention.

mathContext.technique: Existential witness ∅ (empty multiset); simp handles both membership vacuity and Multiset.sum_zero

title: Elements are Self-Representable
content:
**mem_representable**: Any element a ∈ A is representable by A, using the singleton multiset {a}. Proved by `use {a}; simp [ha]`.

This shows A ⊆ RepresentableSet(A), the generating set embeds into its semigroup.

mathContext.technique: Existential witness {a} (singleton multiset); simp with membership hypothesis

title: Sum Closure of Representability
content:
**add_representable**: If m and n are both representable by A, then m + n is too. Combine multisets Sm + Sn: membership follows from cases on Multiset.mem_add, and sum follows from Multiset.sum_add.

This proves the representable set forms a subsemigroup of (ℕ, +). Together with zero_representable, it's a submonoid.

mathContext.technique: Destructs both existentials to get Sm, Sn; witnesses Sm + Sn; membership by cases on Multiset.mem_add; sum by simp with sub-goals
mathContext.proofMethod: Constructive: builds the witness multiset by concatenation
mathContext.keyProperty: This closure under addition is what makes the Frobenius problem interesting: eventually all large enough integers become representable when gcd(A) = 1

title: Non-Representable Set
content:
**NonRepresentable A** = {n : ℕ | ¬IsRepresentableAs n A}, the complement of the representable set within ℕ. When gcd(A) = 1, this set is finite (classical Frobenius theorem). When gcd(A) > 1, infinitely many integers are non-representable.

Problem #434 asks to maximize |NonRepresentable A| by choosing A optimally.

mathContext.technique: Set comprehension with negation of IsRepresentableAs
consequences: nCardNonRepresentable: the ℕ-valued count via Set.ncard

title: Counting Non-Representables
content:
Two counting functions: **countNonRepresentable** (ℕ∞-valued via Set.encard, handles infinite case) and **nCardNonRepresentable** (ℕ-valued via Set.ncard, returns 0 for infinite sets).

Both are noncomputable. The ncard version is used in Kiss's theorem since the interesting case has gcd = 1 (finite non-representables).

mathContext.technique: Set.encard for extended natural cardinality; Set.ncard for natural cardinality (0 when infinite)

title: Frobenius Number
content:
**frobeniusNumber A** = sSup(NonRepresentable A), the largest non-representable integer. Well-defined when gcd(A) = 1 (the set is finite and bounded). For coprime a, b: frobeniusNumber {a,b} = ab - a - b (Sylvester 1884).

Note: Problem #434 maximizes the COUNT, not the Frobenius number itself. Problem #433 focuses on maximizing the Frobenius number.

mathContext.technique: sSup (supremum) of NonRepresentable A; relies on the set being bounded above when gcd(A) = 1

crossReferences.relationship: Problem #433 maximizes the Frobenius number g(k,n) = max{G(A)}, while #434 maximizes the count of non-representables

title: Complete Sets (gcd = 1)
content:
**IsComplete A** holds when A is nonempty and gcd(sSup A, sInf(A \ {sSup A})) = 1. Complete sets have finitely many non-representable integers.

The Chicken McNugget theorem is a famous example: {6, 9, 20} has Frobenius number 43. More practically, the 'coin problem': what amounts can't be made with given coin denominations?

mathContext.technique: Nat.gcd applied to sSup and sInf of the remainder set; a simplified coprimality check
mathContext.historicalNote: The Chicken McNugget theorem (for {6, 9, 20}) became a popular math puzzle. The general Frobenius problem for ≥ 3 elements is NP-hard (Ramírez-Alfonsín 2005).

title: The topK Set: {n-k+1, ..., n}
content:
**topK n k** = Set.Icc (n - k + 1) n, the k largest elements of {1,...,n}. This is the conjectured (and proved) optimal choice for maximizing non-representables.

Examples: topK 5 2 = {4, 5}, topK 10 3 = {8, 9, 10}. The greedy construction greedyConstruct equals topK by definition (rfl).

mathContext.technique: Set.Icc (closed interval) from n-k+1 to n; natural number subtraction requires care
consequences: topK_card: |topK n k| = k when k ≤ n and k > 0 (sorry)

title: The Extremal Frobenius Question
content:
**ExtremalFrobeniusQuestion n k**: For all A ⊆ {1,...,n} with |A| = k, nCardNonRepresentable(A) ≤ nCardNonRepresentable(topK n k). This is the formal statement that topK is optimal.

Kiss (2002) proved this is true for all valid n, k.

mathContext.technique: Universal quantification over sets A with subset and cardinality constraints; comparison via ≤ on nCardNonRepresentable

title: Small Examples: {2,3}, {3,5}, topK(5,2)
content:
Three concrete examples illustrate the pattern:
- **{2, 3}**: NonRepresentable = {1}, Frobenius number 1. Small numbers → few gaps.
- **{3, 5}**: NonRepresentable = {1, 2, 4, 7}, Frobenius number 7. By Sylvester: 3·5 - 3 - 5 = 7, count = (2)(4)/2 = 4.
- **topK(5, 2) = {4, 5}**: Proved by ext + simp + omega. Many more non-representables: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 11, etc.

The topK example has far more non-representables, illustrating why larger numbers are optimal.

mathContext.technique: example_2_3 and example_3_5_frobenius are sorry'd; topK_5_2 proved via ext, simp [topK, Set.Icc], omega
mathContext.proofMethod: topK_5_2 is the only proved example; it reduces set equality to membership characterization via omega

title: Kiss's Theorem (2002): topK is Optimal
content:
**kiss_2002**: For 1 ≤ k ≤ n, ExtremalFrobeniusQuestion n k holds — the set {n-k+1,...,n} maximizes nCardNonRepresentable among all k-element subsets of {1,...,n}.

This is the main result, axiomatized because Kiss's proof requires detailed analysis of representation counts via generating functions and comparison inequalities for different subsets.

mathContext.technique: Stated as axiom; the proof would require generating function analysis and combinatorial comparison arguments
mathContext.whyAxiom: Kiss's proof uses analytic/combinatorial methods comparing representation numbers across different subset choices. Formalizing this would require substantial generating function and inequality infrastructure beyond what's currently available.
mathContext.historicalNote: Kiss, G. (2002). 'On the extremal Frobenius problem in a new aspect'. Ann. Univ. Sci. Budapest. Eötvös Sect. Math., 139-142.

title: Problem #434 Answer: YES
content:
**erdos_434_answer**: Direct corollary of kiss_2002. For all valid n, k and any A ⊆ {1,...,n} with |A| = k, nCardNonRepresentable(A) ≤ nCardNonRepresentable(topK n k).

Proved by exact application of kiss_2002.

mathContext.technique: Direct application: `kiss_2002 n k hn hk hkn`

title: Larger Numbers Create More Gaps
content:
**larger_numbers_fewer_reps**: For n ≥ 2, nCardNonRepresentable({n-1, n}) > nCardNonRepresentable({1, 2}). Since {1, 2} represents everything except 0, while {n-1, n} leaves many gaps (1 through n-2, plus gaps between multiples).

With {1, 2}: the only non-representable positive integer is... none! (1=1, 2=2, 3=1+2, etc.). With {9, 10}: 1-8 are all non-representable, plus 11-17, etc.

mathContext.technique: Sorry'd; would follow from sylvester_count since {1,2} has count 0 and {n-1,n} has count (n-2)(n-1)/2 > 0
mathContext.whyAxiom: The proof requires computing nCardNonRepresentable for specific sets, which depends on the sorry'd sylvester_count

title: Sylvester-Frobenius Theorem and Count Formula
content:
Two classical results axiomatized:
- **sylvester_frobenius**: For coprime a, b > 0, frobeniusNumber {a,b} = ab - a - b.
- **sylvester_count**: The count of non-representables is (a-1)(b-1)/2.

For {3, 5}: Frobenius number = 15 - 3 - 5 = 7, count = (2)(4)/2 = 4.

**consecutive_count** (sorry): For consecutive integers {n-1, n}, the count is (n-2)(n-1)/2, growing quadratically.

mathContext.technique: Both stated as axioms; sylvester_frobenius dates to 1884, the count formula to Sylvester as well
mathContext.whyAxiom: The Sylvester-Frobenius theorem requires careful analysis of which integers are representable as ax + by with x,y ≥ 0. While elementary, the formal proof needs integer arithmetic and case analysis not developed here.
mathContext.historicalNote: Sylvester proved both results in 1884. The count formula (a-1)(b-1)/2 is sometimes called the Sylvester-Frobenius formula. For 3+ elements, computing the Frobenius number is NP-hard (Ramírez-Alfonsín 2005).

title: Greedy Construction Equals topK
content:
**greedyConstruct n k** = Set.Icc (n - k + 1) n, identical to topK by definition. **greedy_eq_topK**: proved by rfl.

The greedy algorithm (always pick the largest available number) naturally produces the topK set, and Kiss's theorem shows this greedy approach is optimal.

mathContext.technique: Definition is identical to topK; equality proved by rfl (definitional equality)
mathContext.keyProperty: The greedy algorithm is optimal for this problem — a rare case where the simple greedy approach gives the provably best answer

title: Finiteness of Non-Representables
content:
**nonrep_finite**: When A has two coprime elements, NonRepresentable A is finite. **topK_finite**: For k ≥ 2 and n ≥ k, NonRepresentable(topK n k) is finite.

Both are sorry'd. The classical result: if gcd(A) = 1, then all sufficiently large integers are representable (the Frobenius number bounds the non-representable set).

mathContext.technique: Sorry'd; would need the Schur/Frobenius theorem that gcd=1 implies finitely many non-representables

crossReferences.relationship: Problem #433 also depends on finiteness of non-representables for coprime sets

title: Connection to Problem #433
content:
**problem433Set n k** = Set.Icc n (n + k - 1), the consecutive integers {n, n+1, ..., n+k-1}. Problem #433 maximizes the Frobenius number for this specific form; #434 maximizes the non-representable count over all k-subsets.

**frobenius_consecutive** (axiom): The Frobenius number for consecutive integers is (n-1)(n+k-1)/k - 1, as studied in Problem #433.

mathContext.technique: Set.Icc for consecutive integer range; frobenius_consecutive axiomatizes the Frobenius number formula

crossReferences.relationship: Direct companion problem: #433 studies Frobenius numbers for consecutive integers, #434 optimizes the subset choice

title: Complete Answer: topK is Optimal
content:
**erdos_434_complete**: For all n ≥ 1, k ≥ 1, k ≤ n, and any A ⊆ {1,...,n} with |A| = k: nCardNonRepresentable(A) ≤ nCardNonRepresentable(topK n k).

Proved by exact application of kiss_2002. This is the definitive answer to Erdős Problem #434.

mathContext.technique: Direct application of kiss_2002 axiom with all parameters

title: topK Achieves Maximum (IsGreatest)
content:
**topK_is_maximum**: Formulates the result using Mathlib's `IsGreatest`: topK achieves the maximum of {nCardNonRepresentable A | A valid}. Sorry'd — requires showing topK is itself valid (⊆ {1,...,n} with |topK| = k) and applying kiss_2002.

This is the strongest formulation: not just 'all others are ≤' but 'topK is in the set AND is the greatest'.

mathContext.technique: IsGreatest over the image set {nCardNonRepresentable A | A : Set ℕ // A ⊆ Set.Icc 1 n ∧ A.ncard = k}
